mcqs.question: How does a God Object typically come into existence?
options: A single upfront design decision to centralize all logic in one class
Many individually-reasonable commits each adding "just one more responsibility" to the class that's already easiest to reach
A required pattern enforced by most object-oriented languages
A deliberate performance optimization to reduce the number of classes loaded at runtime
mcqs.explanation: God Objects accrete gradually — nobody designs one on purpose. Each feature finds it easiest to extend the already-central class, and the responsibilities pile up over time. It isn't a language requirement, and centralizing logic isn't a real performance technique here.

mcqs.question: What's a concrete way to test whether two classes are too tightly coupled?
options: Count how many other files break when you change one class's implementation while keeping its public behavior the same
Count the total number of lines in both classes combined
Check whether both classes are defined in the same file
Check whether either class has more than one public method
mcqs.explanation: Tight coupling is about how much of a change ripples outward for an internal-only edit — if implementation details leak out and force edits elsewhere despite unchanged public behavior, that's the tell. Line count, same-file placement, and method count don't measure coupling at all.

mcqs.question: In the OrderManager refactor, what does extracting PricingService, OrderRepository, and OrderNotifier actually buy, beyond a shorter method?
options: Each collaborator can now be tested, changed, and reasoned about independently, and OrderManager no longer needs to know how a total is calculated
It automatically makes the application run faster at runtime
It removes the need for OrderManager to exist at all
It guarantees the code will never need further refactoring
mcqs.explanation: The value is decoupling: OrderManager now coordinates without owning implementation details, so each piece can change or be tested in isolation. There's no runtime speed guarantee from this restructuring, OrderManager still has a real coordinating role, and no refactor is a permanent fix against future smells.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes a design anti-pattern from a code smell?
options: Anti-patterns are structural, spanning multiple classes or the whole system; smells are local to one method or class
Anti-patterns only apply to functional programming; smells only apply to object-oriented programming
Anti-patterns are always intentional design choices, while smells are always accidental
There is no real difference — the terms are fully interchangeable
mcqs.explanation: Scope is the real distinction: a smell is something you catch reading one file, an anti-pattern is something you catch reading the dependency graph or feeling the pain of a cross-cutting change. Neither is tied to a specific paradigm, and anti-patterns are typically just as unintentional as smells — they accrete rather than get chosen.

mcqs.question: A 900-line class implements a single, well-organized state machine with clear internal structure. Is it necessarily a God Object?
options: No — size alone isn't the test; the question is whether it has multiple unrelated responsibilities, not whether it's long
Yes — any class over roughly 500 lines is a God Object by definition
Yes, but only if it's written in a dynamically typed language
No, because state machines are exempt from all anti-pattern analysis
mcqs.explanation: The God Object test is about unrelated responsibilities piling onto one class, not raw line count — a large, cohesive state machine can be legitimate. There's no fixed line-count threshold, no language exemption rule, and no blanket exemption for state machines either; a state machine could still be a God Object if it also handled unrelated concerns.
